# Conclusion

This project set out to bridge the gap between Vision-Language Navigation research, which typically runs in simulation, and the practical realities of running an end-to-end natural-language-driven navigation pipeline on embedded hardware. Over approximately four months of work, a modular ROS 2 system was designed, implemented, tested, and documented on the Yahboom ROSMASTER X3 PLUS platform. The system accepts natural-language instructions of the form "chair" or "cup of water", performs an arm-mounted camera sweep, runs YOLOv8 nano object detection to ground the instruction in the environment, estimates the target object's world position by fusing the arm servo angle, bounding-box location, and LiDAR range, constructs a 2D occupancy grid together with a 3D RTAB-Map point cloud, and passes the target pose to the path planner.

## Summary of Findings

Several concrete findings emerged over the course of the project.

- **A reliable startup sequence is itself a deliverable.** A significant portion of the early weeks of the project was spent identifying the correct order in which to launch sensor drivers, motor drivers, and SLAM nodes. The resulting five-step sequence — `display_X3.launch.py` → `Mcnamu_driver_X3` → `base_node_X3` (from the `yahboomcar_base_node` package) → `astro_pro_plus.launch.xml` → `x3_rtabmap_depth.launch.py` — now produces a working system in roughly 20 seconds.

- **Hardware-specific details are often undocumented and have to be discovered experimentally.** Several such details were documented in this report: the motor controller lives on `/dev/ttyUSB1` rather than the expected `/dev/ttyUSB0`; the Astra Pro Plus presents a non-standard UVC product ID (`0x050f`) and therefore requires its own launch file rather than the generic Orbbec launch file; the Astra color stream and the arm wrist camera compete for the same `/dev/video0` device and cannot both run simultaneously; the `base_node_X3` executable lives in a separate package (`yahboomcar_base_node`) from the motor driver; and the `ARM_HOME` pose must tilt the shoulder servo forward or the wrist camera will photograph the ceiling.

- **Professor-directed switch from A\* to RRT\* paid off on real maps.** A\* on a $400 \times 400$ grid produces waypoint counts in the hundreds even after smoothing, while RRT\* produces paths with only a handful of waypoints on the same maps. Both planners remain in the codebase for comparative purposes and because A\* serves as the fallback when RRT\* fails.

- **A modular, topic-based architecture enabled independent development and testing of each subsystem.** In particular, the in-node virtual mover made it possible to exercise the full planner-to-execution pipeline without consuming physical motion time, and the dual-camera-source design of the arm-scan component made it possible to test YOLOv8 detection regardless of whether the Astra camera was active.

- **The unified pipeline now completes all twelve integration points.** The
  interface-drift defect that halted the previous evaluation was resolved as predicted, by
  adding `inflated_mask()` to the SLAM module's occupancy-map class and making the planner
  fallback exception-safe. No further design change was required to unblock the final three
  stages.

- **Common-mode reasoning resolved three sensor faults that resisted individual
  diagnosis.** The LiDAR, depth camera, and wrist camera had each been investigated as
  separate driver problems over multiple sessions. Examined together, they shared a single
  cause — insufficient USB bus current — and a powered hub resolved all three with no
  software change. The general lesson is that a device reporting healthy driver status
  while failing to function physically is evidence pointing away from configuration, and
  simultaneous unrelated-seeming faults in independently-powered peripherals warrant a
  common-mode hypothesis before individual investigation.

- - **Algorithmic refinements to RRT\* pay off in proportion to environment complexity.**
  Across 600 trials on the deployment hardware, QuadTree-accelerated neighbour search with
  side-retreat collision escape was essentially level with the brute-force baseline on
  sparse obstacle fields, roughly twice as fast at medium density, and three to eight times
  faster on structurally constrained hand-built maps such as corridors and mazes. The
  refinement is therefore well matched to the workload, since planning cost is highest
  exactly where the advantage is largest — but it is worth noting that on open maps, which
  describe much of the test environment, the added machinery buys almost nothing.


- **Smoothness and latency trade against each other, and the current system is
  latency-bound.** Convex-corridor QP smoothing reduced the curvature proxy roughly
  nineteen-fold, but at a planning-time cost incurred on every replan, against an execution
  benefit that the current constant-velocity waypoint follower does not exploit. The
  variant is retained against future conditions that would reverse that balance.


## Implications

The implications of this work are practical rather than theoretical. A system-level demonstration that a VLN-style perception-and-localization pipeline can be brought up end-to-end on this specific class of hardware (a Jetson-based differential-drive platform with an RGB-D camera, LiDAR, and a six-degree-of-freedom arm) lowers the barrier for future students to extend it. In particular, the map-guided path-planning approach studied in simulation by Mohiuddin [@mohiuddin2025vln] — explicitly identified by the author as awaiting real-world deployment on "a ROSMaster X3 Plus robot equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX" — now has a working base platform to deploy onto. Integrating that semantic-cost formulation into either the A\* or RRT\* planner implemented here would be a natural next step.

More broadly, the project illustrates that a meaningful fraction of the effort in real-world robot deployment lies below the level of published algorithms: in driver selection, device-file management, transform-tree correctness, camera-device arbitration, and mechanical configuration such as arm home pose. Student projects and research deployments benefit from documenting these artifacts as first-class outputs.

## Limitations

Several limitations of the current system should be acknowledged.

- **Sensor stability under autonomous motion is uncharacterized.** The Astra camera has
  been observed to disconnect and re-enumerate when the robot is displaced manually, a
  fault attributed to USB cable strain relief. Whether autonomous `/cmd_vel` motion
  reproduces it is untested. Until it is, any navigation result that depends on the depth
  stream carries an unquantified risk of intermittent sensor loss.

- **The benchmark environments are synthetic.** The planner comparison was executed on the
  deployment hardware, which makes the timings representative, but the occupancy maps were
  built from ray-cast synthetic geometry rather than recorded LiDAR scans. Real scans carry
  noise, spurious returns, and reflective-surface artefacts that synthetic ray casting does
  not reproduce, and these affect the obstacle mask that the planners search over. The
  relative ordering of the variants is unlikely to change, but the absolute timings should
  be treated as a lower bound.

- **The supporting modules are unvalidated on hardware.** Reactive obstacle avoidance, the
  LLM navigation planner, pick-and-place manipulation, and voice input have each been
  exercised only in simulation or dry-run mode. None is active in the live navigation path,
  and voice input in particular has never run against real audio, since no USB microphone
  is connected.


- **Instruction parsing is minimal.** The task node recognizes only instructions that match entries in a fixed task-to-label dictionary (nine entries covering common objects such as chair, bottle, cup, phone, laptop, book, and person). Richer instructions involving relations ("the bottle on the table"), ordinals ("the second chair"), or multi-step actions ("pick up the bottle and put it on the table") are not supported. Recent VLN surveys document a broad shift toward foundation-model-driven embodied planning that could address this limitation [@zhang_vision-and-language_2024; @chen_mapgpt_2024], but integrating such systems was out of scope for the present engineering-focused project.

- **No formal success benchmark has been run.** The end-to-end pipeline has been demonstrated working up to and including RRT\* invocation on a representative task, but a large-scale evaluation with many trials across different objects, starting positions, and room configurations has not been performed.

- **Detection is purely image-based and single-pass.** If YOLOv8 misses an object at all three arm-sweep positions, the task fails. There is no re-scan, viewpoint-selection, or active-perception strategy. On a real domestic platform this is a significant weakness.

- **Depth estimation is LiDAR-based rather than using the wrist camera.** The wrist camera is monocular, so object distance is inferred from the LiDAR range at the detection bearing. This works well for floor-standing objects but degrades for small tabletop objects, where the LiDAR ray is likely to pass through the object and strike the wall behind it. The system falls back to a default distance of 1.5 m when no valid LiDAR range is present, which is a coarse substitute for real depth.

- **The arm interaction sequence is open-loop.** Once the robot reaches a goal, the arm executes a fixed reach-grip-lift-home sequence at preset servo angles, regardless of the object's measured 3D pose. The gripper closure is not verified, and an unsuccessful grasp is not detected.

- **Odometry is trusted directly.** No sensor fusion between wheel odometry, visual odometry from RTAB-Map, and LiDAR-based odometry is performed. RTAB-Map's pose estimate is used for visualization only and is not fed back into the planner. On longer trajectories, drift accumulates.

## Future Work

The limitations above translate into a prioritized future-work list.

1. **Characterize sensor stability under autonomous motion.** With a collaborator present
   and the Astra USB cable secured for strain relief, drive the robot under `/cmd_vel`
   while monitoring `/scan` and `/camera/depth/image_raw` publication rates for dropout.
   This gates every subsequent result that depends on live perception during motion and
   should therefore precede the benchmark work below.

2. **Integrate neural-guided sampling into the RRT\* planner.** Rather than sampling the
   configuration space uniformly, train a lightweight network to propose samples in regions
   likely to lie on the optimal path, conditioned on the occupancy grid and the start-goal
   pair. Reported reductions in planning time for this class of method fall in the 30–75%
   range. This is the most natural ML contribution for the project: it targets the component
   already established as the system's latency bottleneck, it is evaluable on the existing
   600-trial benchmark harness without modification, and a smaller resulting tree would
   reduce the relative cost of convex-corridor smoothing, potentially making that variant
   viable as the primary planner.

3. **Replace the fixed task-to-label dictionary with a structured-observation LLM subgoal
   planner.** The current nine-entry dictionary admits only single-object instructions. A
   planner that serializes existing YOLO detections and LiDAR ranges into a structured
   textual observation, submits it to a language model, and receives a subgoal coordinate
   would support relational and multi-step instructions while leaving RRT\* as the
   safety-critical executor. This approach requires no model training, and the language
   model runs off-device via an API, so it adds no inference load to the Jetson. It
   subsumes the existing `navgpt_planner.py` work.

4. **Estimate object depth from the wrist camera monocularly.** The current system infers
   object distance from the LiDAR range at the detection bearing, which fails for tabletop
   objects where the ray passes beneath or beside the object and strikes the wall behind.
   A lightweight monocular depth network of the class benchmarked on Jetson-family hardware
   would address the limitation directly, and could be fused with the LiDAR estimate rather
   than replacing it.

5. **Run a formal end-to-end success-rate benchmark.** Define 30–50 natural-language tasks
   across a known object set and room configurations, execute each three times from a fresh
   SLAM map, and report success rate, per-class detection rate, planning failure rate, and
   completion time. This is the principal quantitative gap remaining in the evaluation.

6. **Activate the reactive obstacle avoider beneath the planner.** The module is written
   and simulation-verified but not in the live path. A planner replanning on a fixed
   interval cannot respond to an obstacle appearing between replans, which is exactly the
   gap the avoider is designed to close.

7. **Connect a USB microphone and add wake-word gating to voice input.** The Whisper
   pipeline is implemented but has never run against live audio. Wake-word gating is
   required regardless, since continuous transcription is impractical.

8. **Close the loop on manipulation.** Verify grasp success through gripper-servo current
   sensing or contact sensing, and retry on failure. The pick-and-place module's
   inverse-kinematics solution provides the pose conditioning; what is missing is the
   feedback signal.
